# RG10 `no-baseline`: The impact is measured without a before-value

<!-- Generated by `realism-gate explain --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

**Severity:** warn (warn)

A directional assertion (greater than, less than) checks a balance or state read that happens once, after the attack. Nothing records what it was before.

## Why it matters

`assertGt(token.balanceOf(attacker), 0)` passes if the attacker already had tokens: from `deal`, from a fork's existing holdings, from a `setUp()` transfer. A gain is a difference. Without the earlier read, the PoC cannot tell the exploit's effect from the starting state, and neither can the reader.

## How to fix it

Read the same quantity before and after, and assert on the difference.

## Fires on

```solidity
_attack();
assertGt(token.balanceOf(attacker), 0);
```

## Does not fire on

```solidity
uint256 before = token.balanceOf(attacker);
_attack();
assertGt(token.balanceOf(attacker), before);
```

## How it can be wrong

- A directional claim that is meaningful on its own, such as "the attacker ends with more than the vault's whole TVL". Exact-value assertions (`assertEq`), upper bounds of zero ("drained") and `require` guards are already exempt; for anything else, an `allow` comment saying why the absolute value suffices.
- A baseline taken through a differently written expression (a local alias of the token). Read it the same way both times.

## In Solana tests (Rust and Anchor TypeScript)

A directional assertion (`assert!(a > b)`, `expect(a).to.be.greaterThan(b)`, `assert.isAbove`) checks a balance read once, after the attack: `get_balance` / `getBalance`, a `.lamports` or `.amount` field, or a helper whose name says balance or amount.

**How to fix it:** Read the same quantity before and after, and assert on the difference.

### Fires on

```rust
svm.send_transaction(exploit_tx).unwrap();
assert!(token_balance(&svm, &attacker_tokens) > 0);
```

```typescript
await program.methods.withdraw(new BN(100)).accounts({ recipient: attacker.publicKey }).signers([attacker]).rpc();
const account = await getAccount(provider.connection, attackerTokens);
expect(Number(account.amount)).to.be.greaterThan(0);
```

### Does not fire on

```rust
let before = token_balance(&svm, &attacker_tokens);
svm.send_transaction(exploit_tx).unwrap();
assert!(token_balance(&svm, &attacker_tokens) > before);
```

```typescript
const balanceBefore = (await getAccount(provider.connection, attackerTokens)).amount;
await program.methods.withdraw(new BN(100)).accounts({ recipient: attacker.publicKey }).signers([attacker]).rpc();
const balanceAfter = (await getAccount(provider.connection, attackerTokens)).amount;
expect(Number(balanceAfter)).to.be.greaterThan(Number(balanceBefore));
```

### Known false-positive modes

- A baseline read through a differently written expression (a second helper, an alias). Read it the same way both times.
- A directional claim that is meaningful on its own. Exact-value assertions (`assert_eq!`) and upper bounds of zero are already exempt; for anything else, an `allow` comment saying why the absolute value suffices.

## In Move tests (Sui and Aptos)

`assert!(coin::value(...) > 0)` or `assert!(balance > 0)` with no earlier `coin::value` or `balance` read stored as a before-value.

**How to fix it:** Read the same quantity before and after, and assert on the difference.

### Fires on

```move
#[test]
fun test_profit_without_a_before() {
    let attacker = @0xA11CE;
    test_scenario::next_tx(&mut scenario, attacker);
    vault::withdraw();
    assert!(coin::value(&attacker_coin) > 0, 0);
}
```

### Does not fire on

```move
#[test]
fun test_profit_against_a_before() {
    let attacker = @0xA11CE;
    test_scenario::next_tx(&mut scenario, attacker);
    let before = coin::value(&attacker_coin);
    vault::withdraw();
    assert!(coin::value(&attacker_coin) > before, 0);
}
```

### How it can be wrong

- A before-value read through a different helper than the assertion uses. Read it the same way both times, or add an `allow` comment.

## Silencing it

An `allow` comment in the repo under review does not silence this rule, and neither does a `realism.yaml` or `realism-gate.toml` inside that repo. Policy is an operator file outside the tree (`--declaration`, `--config`). `--trust-inline-allows` is the author switch, for a PoC you wrote and are not gating.

```solidity
// realism-gate: allow(RG10) <why this is not a defect here>
```

The comment is the same in Rust, TypeScript and Move. A comment without a reason is ignored even with `--trust-inline-allows`, and the output says so.
